stories.title: South Africa's Ramaphosa wins court battle over impeachment threat
stories.summary: Image source, Gallo via Getty Images Image caption, President Cyril Ramaphosa has faced calls to resign over his handling of the "Farmgate" scandal By Khanyisile Ngcobo Reporting from Johannesburg Published 25 November 2026, 06:41 GMT Updated 33 minutes ago South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has won a legal battle to overturn a report that found he may have a case to answer over the theft of large sums of cash from his private farm. In 2022, an independent panel said Ramaphosa may have committed serious misconduct relating to the theft of $580,000 (Â£443,000), hidden in a sofa, at his Phala Phala game farm in the Limpopo province. Ramaphosa challenged the findings of the report in court after the Constitutional Court ruled that parliament had violated the constitution by blocking moves to impeach him. The Western Cape high court ruled that the panel's report was unlawful and set it aside "in its entirety". In its judgment, the court said the panel, appointed by parliament to investigate the allegations against Ramaphosa, had "misconstrued its function, the nature of the inquiry it was to conduct and the recommendation it was required to make". "It went beyond its lawful remit ... and made several material errors of law. [Therefore] the report of the independent panel ... is declared unlawful and is reviewed and set aside in its entirety," Judge Nolwazi Mabindla-Boqwana said.

stories.title: Swiss tourist killed and British and Americans injured by elephants in Cameroon
stories.summary: 2:09 British tourists interviewed after elephants kill Swss hiker in Mt Cameroon trek Swiss tourist killed and British and Americans injured by elephants in Cameroon Alain Throo, insurance executive based in London, reportedly gored and later died on hike near Mount Cameroon national park A Swiss tourist has been killed and British and American tourists have been injured when a group of hikers encountered a herd of elephants in Cameroon . The group of six tourists, four British, one Swiss and one American, accompanied by local guides, were hiking near the village of Bakingili in the south of the Mount Cameroon national park on 19 November, on a path used by elephants to access a nearby lake, when they encountered the herd of about 15 animals, according to media reports. The elephants attacked the group and Alain Throo, a Swiss insurance executive based in London, was reportedly gored and one of the guides tossed into a ditch on top of Throo, while the others hid in trees. Throo had a black eye and was initially responsive and complaining about an injury to his arm, one of the British female hikers told Cameroonian media, which said they had feared he was bleeding internally. “He said that the elephant attacked him,” an unidentified Cameroonian man added, according to a video posted by CBS Radio Buea FM. “It smashed him.” View image in fullscreen An African forest elephant. Photograph: Danita Delimont/Alamy Throo later died of his injuries and his body was carried out of the park by a combined team of park staff and the military to a mortuary in the town of Limbeon 21 November.

The government wants its empowerment policies to help more black business owners manufacture products, supply goods and sell them to other countries. South Africa will not give up its black economic empowerment policies to secure lower tariffs from the United States. Minister of Trade, Industry and Competition Parks Tau made this clear during the Broad-Based Black Economic Empowerment (B-BBEE) Practice and Policy Conference in Johannesburg on Monday. Relations between South Africa and the US remain strained, with Washington raising concerns about the country's economic empowerment policies.

stories.title: East Africa: Somalia's Parliament Speaker Accuses Kenya, Ethiopia, Uganda of Colluding With Al-Shabaab
stories.summary: East Africa: Somalia's Parliament Speaker Accuses Kenya, Ethiopia, Uganda of Colluding With Al-Shabaab AU-UN IST Photo / Stuart Price A Ugandan soldier service with the African Union Mission (file photo). 25 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Somalia's parliamentary speaker Abdulkadir Mohamed Nur, also known as Jaamac, has accused Kenya, Ethiopia and Uganda of colluding with Al-Shabaab, alleging that Israel had brought together the three countries, the militant group and forces loyal to former South West State leader Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Laftagareen in a coordinated front against the federal government. Nur made the accusations on 24 November while closing a conference on Somalia's productive resources organized by Magan Forum in Mogadishu. He warned that unnamed foreign powers were seeking to recolonize Somalia and urged Somalis to defend the country's sovereignty. The allegations, which remain unsubstantiated but were reported widely by Somali local media, risk further straining relations with regional partners involved in Somalia's security efforts. The remarks build on Nur's earlier accusations against neighboring countries and the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM).

The man, who was from Sri Lanka and had a history of severe mental illness and suicide attempts, took his own life months after arriving in Eswatini. stories.title: Ghost strikes: the new drone superpowers raining death from above
stories.summary: Warning: contains graphic content some readers may find upsetting Scroll to continue Still, as he lost consciousness again, he was sure who they were. “I knew they were my daughters, because the body parts strewn out in the cave were so small.” Ghost strikes: the new drone superpowers raining death from above The spread of cheap drones means warfare is increasingly conducted by invisible armies at the push of a button. Victims have no warning and no chance for justice Death had come from the sky for Mohamed’s family: an execution carried out with no warning, no trial, no guilty verdict or chance for recourse. He did not even know who had carried out the killing, or under which authority – several nations have drones patrolling the skies of Somalia looking for Islamic State militants, including the US, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Turkey and the Somali government. The campaign, launched on 21 November, is being conducted in Addis Abeba, Oromia, Central Ethiopia, South Ethiopia, and Southwest Ethiopia regions in collaboration with the World Health Organization (WHO), UNICEF, the Global Polio Eradication Initiative (GPEI), and other partners. The first round runs from 21-24 November, with a second round scheduled for 18-21 December. Vaccination teams comprising health workers and community volunteers are conducting house-to-house visits to administer polio vaccines and reach eligible children. In a statement published yesterday, the organisation has warned of escalating violations against women and girls as fighting intensifies, with thousands of families fleeing their homes and facing growing humanitarian risks. SIHA Network says it has received confirmed reports that 28 women and girls were abducted while attempting to flee Damazin. It also reported 15 cases of conflict-related sexual violence against girls under the age of 18, warning of an escalation in violations against women and girls following renewed fighting in the region. In a report seen by Radio Dabanga, the organisation said fighters from the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and allied militias had abducted the women and girls as they attempted to reach safer areas.

stories.title: Africa: Decades of Gains Against Aids Could Unravel As HIV Funding Dries Up
stories.summary: Africa: Decades of Gains Against Aids Could Unravel As HIV Funding Dries Up Jay Caboz/Bhekisisa Lenacapavir, the six-monthly anti-HIV jab. 24 November 2026 UN News Service Decades of progress against AIDS, one of the greatest public health achievements in history, could go into reverse as international HIV funding is cut and campaigns against human rights and gender equality gain ground, the UN agency devoted to ending the pandemic warned Tuesday in a new report . HIV, the virus that attacks the immune system and causes AIDS, was once a death sentence. Life-saving medicines have turned it into a manageable health condition, allowing millions of people to live with it. Some 32.1 million of the 40 million people living with HIV are now on treatment , but there is currently a $4.3 billion funding gap in low and middle-income countries between available resources and what is needed to keep up these strong results. Kenya appears to be in a constant state of electioneering, with campaigns starting as soon as new leaders are sworn in and intensifying as the next election approaches. The federation also faulted CAS for what it considered a failure to adequately address the regulations governing players who leave the pitch without the referee's authorisation.

stories.title: Africa: One in Six Pregnancies Is to an Adolescent Girl, Yet Only One Health Facility in Eight Offers Services Built for Young People - New Africa CDC Report
stories.summary: One in Six Pregnancies Is to an Adolescent Girl, Yet Only One Health Facility in Eight Offers Services Built for Young People - New Africa CDC Report 22 November 2026 Content from a Premium Partner Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Addis Ababa) "Seen, Served and Counted", a continental assessment of adolescent health drawing on data from the Ministries of Health of all 55 African Union Member States, was launched at the Africa CDC Youth Pre-Conference and Women in Health Leadership Summit ADDIS ABABA, Ethiopia, 22 November 2026 - Africa's health systems are failing to reach the continent's 10- to 19-year-olds, not for lack of policy but for lack of delivery, financing and data. That is the finding of Seen, Served and Counted: The State of Adolescent Health in African Union Member States , launched today by the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC). In the countries able to report, pregnancies among girls aged 10 to 19 make up 16.5% of all pregnancies, rising to 24.2% in Southern Africa, almost one in four. Five years of effort have moved that share only slightly, from 17.9% in 2021. Yet only 12.9% of health facilities offered adolescent- and youth-friendly services in 2025, with almost no change since 2021.

stories.summary: Image source, Family handout Image caption, Okuhle's body was found dumped near a river in August. It was August and he hadn't been able to reach 27-year-old Okuhle for days, although it wasn't unusual for her to drop out of contact from time to time. Then one Saturday, two of Tuku's neighbours called him to say that they had seen that Okuhle had been reported missing by police on Facebook. stories.title: Africa: In Tokyo, Dr Sidi Ould Tah Calls On Japanese Companies to Invest More in Local Value Addition to African Resources
stories.summary: In Tokyo, Dr Sidi Ould Tah Calls On Japanese Companies to Invest More in Local Value Addition to African Resources 23 November 2026 Content from a Premium Partner African Development Bank (Abidjan) African Development Bank Group President Dr Sidi Ould Tah has called on Japanese companies to invest more in the local processing and beneficiation of African resources, assuring that the Bank Group is ready to mobilise financing and risk-sharing instruments to support these investments. He was speaking at a business roundtable organised by the Bank Group in collaboration with the Japanese private sector in Tokyo on 12 November, during his second official visit to Japan as President. Dr Ould Tah outlined three investment priorities: promoting Africa's natural resources and creating greater value on the continent; developing the energy, transport and digital infrastructure essential for industrialisation; and harnessing Japanese technology and finance to support African businesses and bankable projects on the continent. Addressing a large gathering of Japanese business leaders and representatives of private financial institutions and development finance institutions (DFIs), Dr Ould Tah said, "Africa has the resources, markets and talent needed to become a major production hub. But this future will not be built solely on the export of raw materials." He invited them to forge a new generation of investment partnerships to transform African resources into added value, jobs and competitive industries.

Photograph: Chris Scarffe/Courtesy of Madagasikara Voakajy How a tiny rare frog became an ecological warning sign for Madagascar The golden mantella is said to be found wherever gold is, making its habitat a target for illegal mining, which is destroying fragile ecosystems across the country A s Albert Rakotoarisoa emerges from the forest into a clearing in Mangabe reserve in the east of Madagascar , he sees dozens of holes dug in the marshy ground, a sign that people have been here to search for gold. “I came a couple of weeks ago, and these weren’t here,” he says as he surveys the damage, counting 40 holes. “I’m really disappointed.” Rakotoarisoa, 52, patrols the area regularly on behalf of a local group of volunteers and Madagasikara Voakajy, an organisation that protects the island’s endemic species and their habitats.

He hopes his age will stand in his favour as he campaigns for a seat in the state assembly in the northern Kano state in January's general elections. stories.title: More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged
stories.summary: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Africa is pushing for adaptation finance to be tripled by 2035, from an annual $40bn (Â£30bn) By Navin Singh Khadka Environmental correspondent, BBC World Service Published 20 November 2026 In Uganda's northern Karamoja region, Elijah Lobur and his family now eat just one meal a day. A severe drought that began in April has destroyed crops, while food brought in from elsewhere has become increasingly unaffordable. "Seven months without rain has brought us to this point where we now live in hunger," the 44-year-old farmer, who lives with his grandmother, wife and five children, told the BBC. "Even some of the wild plants that we used to eat have withered and dried up." Local officials say more than 90% of crops have failed in the region, where agriculture is largely rain-fed. Further south, in Malawi, Mathews Nkhambala has experienced the devastating effects of flooding. In April 2024, barely a year after Tropical Cyclone Freddy devastated the country's southern region, floods displaced people in Chikwawa district. Nkhambala fled to higher ground with his wife and four children as floodwaters swept through his village. "As we reached a safe height, we saw our house swept away right in front of our eyes.

stories.title: Race to replant five South African baobabs after export blocked
stories.summary: Sarah Venter, founder of the Baobab Foundation, with one of the baobabs to be transported to Timbavati reserve in north-eastern South Africa. Photograph: Courtesy of Timbavati nature reserve View image in fullscreen Sarah Venter, founder of the Baobab Foundation, with one of the baobabs to be transported to Timbavati reserve in north-eastern South Africa. Photograph: Courtesy of Timbavati nature reserve Race to replant five South African baobabs after export blocked The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permits Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia. The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa , on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions.

stories.title: Mentors, colleagues and friends: tributes paid to the ‘Eritrea 16’ who disappeared 25 years ago
stories.summary: The Eritrea 16 were imprisoned without trial in 2001, along with 12 writers, held incommunicado since 2001, and hundreds of conscientious objectors. Photograph: Courtesy of CPJ Africa View image in fullscreen The Eritrea 16 were imprisoned without trial in 2001, along with 12 writers, held incommunicado since 2001, and hundreds of conscientious objectors. Photograph: Courtesy of CPJ Africa Mentors, colleagues and friends: tributes paid to the ‘Eritrea 16’ who disappeared 25 years ago Families of journalists who vanished into state prisons on ‘Black Tuesday’ in 2001 do not know whether they are even still alive When Fisseha Yirgalem stepped on to the podium and began reading from a letter written to a man who may never hear it, the room full of journalists in Nairobi fell quiet. The Eritrean writer’s personal tribute to Amanuel Asrat , a poet, writer, and founder of Zemen newspaper, was not merely about an abstract human rights case but about her mentor, former colleague and friend whose life had in effect been erased by the authoritarian state of Eritrea. Asrat is one of 16 journalists who disappeared into Eritrea’s prison system 25 years ago on Black Tuesday – 18 September 2001 – when the government shut down all of the newspapers in the country.

stories.title: One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN
stories.summary: Seven countries in Africa expressly exempt husbands from prosecution for marital rape, including Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia and South Sudan. Photograph: Frank Dejongh/Unicef View image in fullscreen Seven countries in Africa expressly exempt husbands from prosecution for marital rape, including Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia and South Sudan. Photograph: Frank Dejongh/Unicef One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report. In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund ( UNFPA ) published on Thursday.
